Dear Sir or Madam,


(1)    On 21 May 2026, the European Commission received notification of a proposed
        concentration pursuant to Article 4 of the Merger Regulation by which Baker
       Hughes Company (‘BH’, United States) will acquire within the meaning of
         Article 3(1)(b) of the Merger Regulation sole control of Chart Industries, Inc.
         (‘Chart’, United States) (the ‘Transaction’). (3) (BH and Chart are designated as
         ‘the Parties’.)

1.    THE PARTIES
(2)   BH is a US-based global energy technology company that provides various
        products and services to the oil and gas industry. Of particular relevance to the
        Transaction is its compressor business, as BH designs, manufactures, sells and
         services various types of compressors for a wide range of applications in the
        energy industry (including the compression of liquefied natural gas, ‘LNG’). BH
         also markets prefabricated liquefaction modules, which integrate  all of the
       components needed for liquefaction of natural gas in one prefabricated structure.
(3)     Chart is a US company involved in the design, engineering, and manufacturing of
        process technologies and equipment for gas and liquid molecule handling for
        power, water, food, and industrial applications. In the area of liquefaction of
         natural gas, Chart licences plant process technology and supplies main cryogenic
        heat exchangers (‘MCHE’). While Chart also has various types of compressors in
           its offer, these are not the compressors used in the liquefaction of natural gas.


2.    THE CONCENTRATION
(4)    On 28 July 2025, the Parties entered into an agreement under which BH will
        acquire all outstanding shares of Chart’s common stock (the ‘Transaction’). BH
         will thus acquire sole control over Chart. It follows that the Transaction is a
        concentration within the meaning of Article 3(1)(b) of the Merger Regulation.


3.    UNION DIMENSION
(5)     The undertakings concerned have a combined aggregate world-wide turnover of
       more than EUR 5 000 million (4). Each of them has a Union-wide turnover in
        excess of EUR 250 million, but each does not achieve more than two-thirds of its
        aggregate Union-wide turnover within one and the same Member State. The
         notified operation therefore has a Union dimension within the meaning of
         Article 1(2) of the Merger Regulation.


4.    OVERVIEW OF THE LNG SECTOR AND THE PARTIES’ ACTIVITIES
(6)      Liquefaction is the process of cooling natural gas to condense it into liquid natural
        gas (LNG). This process reduces the volume of gas significantly making  it
        economically viable to transport over long distances. Liquefaction takes place in
        gas-exporting areas. The resulting LNG is then typically shipped via specialised
     LNG carriers to gas-importing regions, where  it is regasified at LNG import
         terminals by warming  it back  into  its gaseous  state. Unlike  liquefaction,
         regasification does not require cryogenic refrigeration but the controlled addition
        of heat. Following regasification, the natural gas is injected into the transmission
        network for onward transportation and distribution to industrial, commercial and
         residential end users.
(7)     While liquefaction occurs mainly outside the EEA (5), the EEA is one of the main
         net importers of LNG globally, together with China, Japan, South Korea, India
       and Taiwan. Unlike major LNG exporting countries, the EEA has very limited

        producer/exporter of natural gas. The only large-scale liquefaction facility in the
     EEA is the Hammerfest LNG plant in Norway, where a few smaller scale
         liquefaction facilities are also located. By contrast, the EEA has an extensive
        network of LNG import and regasification terminals, which enables injection into
         the gas transmission network for onward distribution to the end users.
(8)     The importance of LNG in the European gas supply mix has been increasing over
         the last decade. Natural gas currently represents around 20% of the EU’s overall
        energy consumption. In 2024, about 22% of that gas was used in the electricity
       and heat generation sector, and around 38% in industry. Most of the rest is used
         in the residential and services sectors, mainly for heating buildings. In this
         context, LNG’s share of the EU’s total gas imports has more than doubled over
         the recent years, from 20% in 2021 to 45% in 2025. (6)
(9)     Access to affordable LNG is of strategic importance to the EU. Geopolitical
         disruptions in recent years have put upward pressure on European gas prices
         overall and increased the EU’s reliance on LNG.
(10)    The Russian war of aggression on Ukraine in 2022 accelerated the EU’s efforts
         to phase out Russian fossil fuels, leading to an increase in LNG imports as a more
         flexible and geographically diversified supply source. Phased out Russian gas
        imports have been replaced mainly by LNG from the US, which supplied 58% of
     EU LNG imports in 2025 and pipeline gas imports from Norway (54% compared
         to 30% in 2021), North-Africa (19%), United Kingdom (8%) and Azerbaijan
        (7%). (7)

4.1.    Development of LNG projects
(11)   LNG is produced by compressing natural gas and then cooling it to cryogenic
        temperatures at -162°C, which transforms the gas into a liquid. The liquefaction
        process reduces the gas volume to 1/600th of its gaseous state, which makes it
         easier to transport. (8)
(12)    The construction of LNG plants is highly capital-intensive, and financing is
         typically contingent on the prior negotiation of the plant’s supply arrangements,
        providing sufficient certainty regarding the recovery of capital and operating
         expenditures. (9) LNG plants generally operate either under a tolling model,
       whereby the plant charges a liquefaction fee for processing natural gas supplied
       by the customer, or under a merchant model, whereby the plant operator owns the
         gas, liquefies it, and sells the resulting LNG on the market. (10) In both cases, the
       commercial terms governing the sale of LNG volumes committed under long-
        term agreements agreed before financing for the construction of the plant is
         obtained. (11)
(13)    The core of an LNG plant consists of the so-called ‘liquefaction train’, where the
         natural gas is transformed from a gaseous state to a liquid. An LNG plant includes

(15)    The main parts of an LNG liquefaction train are the following (13):
          (a)   the process technology, which refers to the overall design and engineering
            framework of a liquefaction unit, meaning the process through which
               natural gas is cooled and converted into a liquid. It defines and directs how
              the different components of the liquefaction train work together. There are
               different process technologies for LNG liquefaction trains, depending on
              the technical configuration and the process technology vendor’s design for
              the  liquefaction  train. During  the  planning  of an LNG  plant,  the
              Engineering, Procurement and Construction (‘EPC’) company or plant
            owner selects the process technology at an early stage because that is what
              defines how the plant operates and largely determines the selection of the
             equipment that together will make up the liquefaction train;
         (b)   the main refrigerant compressor train (14). This is a compressor typically
              driven by either a gas turbine or an electric motor, which compresses a
              cooling gas (typically a mixed refrigerant involving a blend of different
              molecules); (15)

(14)   LNG plants also utilise auxiliary compressor trains, which are not part of the liquefaction train or

(15)    The precise process can vary and involve a single refrigeration cycle (as is done for single mixed
         refrigerant processes, such as that used by Chart), two refrigeration cycles (dual-mixed refrigerant
         processes) a pre-cooling stage using propane first followed by a mixed refrigerant cycle, or a
        cascade process using pure separate refrigerants rather than mixed refrigerants in three circuits to

             compressed cooling gas is fed into one or more heat exchangers, which
               transfer heat from the natural gas to the cooling gas, thereby cooling the
               natural gas until it condenses into LNG. As shown in Figure 1 and discussed

              technologies used in LNG liquefaction  trains: brazed aluminium heat
             exchangers (“BAHX”), which consist of stacked layers of aluminium fins
            and parting sheets, brazed together into a single core compact, and coil
           wound heat exchangers (“CWHE”), which are based on coils of tubing
           wound around a central core. In order to achieve the capacity requirements
              of a liquefaction train, multiple BAHX can be grouped into a “cold box”.

                built in a single exchanger to accommodate whatever capacity is required;

(16)   BH and Chart have largely complementary  portfolios with respect  to the
        technology and equipment used to liquefy natural gas.
(17)   BH  is  the incumbent  supplier of compressor  trains  for LNG production.
        According to BH, it is the most referenced OEM for LNG plants, supplying large
        gas turbines and main refrigerant compressors.  (16) BH's turbomachinery  is
         installed in […] LNG plants in operation or under construction worldwide,
         representing more than […] Tonnes Per Annum (MTPA) of global installed LNG
         capacity. BH also offers prefabricated modules (see Section 6.5) (17), which
         integrate BH’s compressor trains and process technology with other components
        sourced from  third  parties, including MCHE. BH does not market LNG
         liquefaction process technology standalone but integrates its open source-based
        process technology in the prefabricated modules that it offers.
(18)    Chart is both active as a supplier of MCHE and as a licensor of process technology
         in the LNG industry. In particular, Chart only supplies one type of MCHE, namely
      BAHX, that can be grouped into cold boxes (see paragraph (51) (18)). It holds a
        long-standing presence in the market for the supply of BAHX dating back to

         for use with Chart’s cold boxes. Chart does not licence IPSMR on a standalone
         basis but only with its BAHX cold boxes. Conversely, Chart offers BAHX cold
        boxes both on a standalone basis and as part of an integrated offering with

(19)   LNG plant owners include international and national oil companies, such as

(20)     Plant owners often outsource the development of an LNG plant  to EPC

       manage  all  aspects  of  construction  throughout  the  project’s development

        planned liquefaction train.
(21)    While the compressor train, MCHE and process technology each fulfil a distinct

        procurement process as it determines the interaction of all the main components
        of the liquefaction train. For this reason, it is typically selected first.
(22)    Once the process technology has been selected, the liquefaction train equipment
         (including the compressor train and MCHE) is selected later by tender or bilateral
         negotiations with suppliers. (22)


5.    RELEVANT MARKETS
(23)    The main products relevant for the competitive assessment of this Transaction are
           (i) the supply of main refrigerant compressors for liquefaction of natural gas, (ii)
         the supply of prefabricated modules for liquefaction of natural gas by BH, (iii) the
        supply of LNG process technologies and (iv) LNG MCHE (23) for liquefaction of
         natural gas by Chart. These products are closely related, meaning that the
        Transaction leads to conglomerate links between the Parties’ activities.
(24)    The Transaction also results in overlaps or vertical relationships for a number of
         other markets. However, all of these overlaps and vertical relationships do not
        give rise to affected markets as a result of the application of the Notice on
        Simplified Procedure. (24) Therefore, these markets will not be further discussed
         in this Decision.

5.1.    Product market definitions

5.1.1.   Compressor trains
(25)   A compressor train typically consists of one or more compressors and a driver,
         together with the associated auxiliary systems. Compressor trains are used to
       compress and circulate refrigerant gases throughout the LNG plant. They increase
        gas pressure to enable cooling in order to liquefy natural gas and to maintain the
        pressure and flow conditions required for efficient and reliable plant operation.
       The driver supplies the mechanical power necessary to operate the compressor
       and may consist of a gas turbine, steam turbine, or electric motor, depending on
         the plant design.

5.1.1.1. Commission’s precedents
(26)    In its past decisional practice, the Commission concluded that the relevant product
        market in oil and gas is the entire compressor train rather than compressors on
          their own. (25)
(27)    The Commission has previously assessed the product market definition for
        compressor trains in the oil and gas industry and considered a distinct product
        market for compressor trains driven by light industrial gas turbines and aero
         derivate gas turbines. (26) The Commission considered a further segmentation by
       power requirement above and below 23 MW but ultimately  left the exact
         definition  open. (27) However,  the Commission’s  practice  does  not  refer
         specifically to compressor trains for use in LNG plants.

5.1.1.2. Notifying Party’s views
(28)    The Notifying Party submits that there is no separate market for compressors and
         drivers, which are typically supplied together as part of a compressor trains, but
         rather form part of a broader market for compressor trains. (28)
(29)    Likewise, in the Notifying Party’s view, there is no separate market(s) specifically
         for compressor trains for LNG plants. Instead, it is submitted that compressor
          trains for LNG plants form part of a broader market for compressor trains serving
        a range of applications in the oil and gas sector and other industrial processes. In
       any event, according to the Notifying Party, the market definition can be left open,
         since there is no affected market. (29)
(30)    Nor, in the Notifying Party’s view, is any further segmentation warranted on the
         basis of the size of the compressor trains, the LNG plant’s capacity or the type of
         driver. (30)

5.1.1.3. Commission’s assessment
(31)    The Commission’s market investigation confirms that compressor trains must be
        considered as a relevant systems market as compressors and drivers are procured
         together. Compressor train suppliers overwhelmingly confirmed that compressors
       and drivers for LNG liquefaction are typically procured together as an integrated
        compressor train package. (31) Likewise, the majority of responding plant owners
       and EPC  contractors  submit  that  they  (or  their  clients)  usually  procure
        compressors and drivers for LNG liquefaction plants together. (32)
(32)      It appears that the procurement of a compressor train consisting of a compressor
       and a driver is often the most efficient approach. (33) In the market investigation,
         plant owners explained that they prefer to procure both components as an
         integrated compressor train as it minimizes the risk of integration between both
       components and they can rely on one other party that takes over the responsibility
         for the train’s operation. (34) Further, plant owners named several other factors
        supporting  this  finding such  as  interface  design, performance  guarantees,
        warranty coverage and risk mitigation. (35)
(33)     Further, the Commission finds that compressor trains to liquefy natural gas cannot
        be substituted with compressor trains used for other applications. The market
         investigation confirms that compressor trains used to liquefy natural gas must be
         specifically designed for the LNG specific use case. (36) This view was supported
         in the market investigation by a large majority of compressor train suppliers for
     LNG liquefaction plants and of EPC contractors. (37) Even if it may be technically
         possible to adapt other compressors trains for LNG liquefaction, it is usually not
        commercially  viable due  to  the  high  costs  associated  with  the  required
         modifications. (38) One compressor train supplier explained that in “most LNG
         liquefaction  applications,  simply  substituting  compressor  trains  (or  their
        components) with ones not specifically designed for LNG service is high-risk and
         often impractical without major modification, re-rating and validation”. (39)
(34)    The market investigation also assessed whether a distinction should be made
       between main refrigerant compressor trains for LNG end applications depending
       on the size of the liquefaction train, on the one hand, or the technology of the
        compressor driver, on the other. The results indicate that gas-turbine driven
        compressor trains remain the standard solution for large-scale and extra-large
     LNG liquefaction trains, while electric motor driven compressor trains are ideally
        used for small-, mid- and increasingly large-scale applications. By contrast, steam
         turbine-driven compressor trains are largely regarded as a legacy technology and
         are  rarely  used  in new LNG  projects.  Centrifugal  compressors  are  the
        predominant compressor technology across LNG liquefaction plant of all sizes,

5.1.2.  LNG process technology
(39)    Process technology refers to the overall design and engineering framework of a
         liquefaction unit, meaning the process through which natural gas is cooled and
        converted into a liquid. It defines the key engineering parameters, the required
        equipment, and the operating conditions of that equipment.
(40)    The fundamental principles of natural gas liquefaction are broadly understood
        across the industry. Process technology licensors build on these generally known
         principles with proprietary knowhow and, in some cases, patented innovations.
        Their  expertise  lies  in  optimising  process parameters such  as  refrigerant
        compositions, heat integration strategies, and operating envelopes to maximise
         efficiency, reliability and overall performance of the liquefaction process.
(41)    There are several different process technologies for LNG compressor trains that
          differ in terms of their technical requirements. They can be broadly categorised
        as follows: Single mixed-refrigerant Processes (“SMR”, Chart’s IPSMR belong

6.2.1. _ Overview of possible strategies
(109) Based on its investigation, the Commission has found a risk of foreclosure of
Chart’s competitors in the supply of LNG process technologies and LNG MCHE.
(110) Such foreclosure could be achieved through the leveraging of BH’s dominant

reducing interoperability of BH’s compressor trains with third party

(c) applying various other, non-price exclusionary tactics vis-a-vis Chart’s
rivals in the markets for process technology, such as withholding or
delaying key technical compressor train information needed for rivals’ bids,
reducing performance guarantees for LNG plants utilising non-Chart
products, or delaying compressor train delivery to LNG plant projects

6.2.2.   Legal framework for the competitive assessment of conglomerate effects
(112)   According  to  the Non-Horizontal Merger  Guidelines,  in  the  majority  of
        circumstances,  conglomerate  mergers  will  not  lead  to  any  competition
        problems. (92)
(113)   However, foreclosure effects may arise when the combination of products in
         related markets may confer on the merged entity the ability and incentive to
        leverage a strong market position from one market to another closely related
        market by means of tying or bundling or other exclusionary practices. While tying
       and  bundling  have  often  no  anticompetitive  consequences,  in  certain
        circumstances such practices may lead to a reduction in actual or potential
        competitors’ ability or incentive to compete. This may reduce the competitive
        pressure on the merged entity allowing it to increase prices. (93)
(114)   In assessing the likelihood of such a scenario, the Commission examines, first,
        whether the merged firm would have the ability to foreclose its rivals, (94) second,
        whether it would have the economic incentive to do so (95) and, third, whether a
         foreclosure strategy would have a significant detrimental effect on competition,
        thus causing harm to consumers. (96) In practice, these factors are often examined
         together as they are closely intertwined.
(115)   In order to be able to foreclose competitors, the merged entity must have a
         significant degree of market power, which does not necessarily amount to
        dominance, in one of the markets concerned. The effects of bundling or tying can
        only be expected to be substantial when at least one of the merging parties’
        products is viewed by many customers as particularly important and there are few
         relevant alternatives for that product. (97) Further, for foreclosure to be a potential
        concern, it must be the case that there is a large common pool of customers, which
           is more likely to be the case when the products are complementary. (98) Finally,
        bundling is less likely to lead to foreclosure if rival firms are able to deploy
         effective and  timely  counter-strategies, such  as  single-product companies
       combining their offers. (99)
(116)   The incentive to foreclose rivals through bundling or tying depends on the degree
         to which this strategy is profitable. (100) Bundling and tying may entail losses or
        foregone revenues for the merged entity. (101) However, they may also allow the
       merged entity to increase profits by gaining market power in the tied goods

(207)   Based on the evidence on the Commission’s file, including the results of the
        market investigation, the Commission considers that BH would likely have the
         incentive to engage in foreclosure strategies with regard to competing providers
        of LNG process technology and LNG MCHE. The incentives for the merged
         entity to engage in these foreclosure strategies depend on the trade-off between
          lost sales in the compressor trains market and the gains it could derive from
        favouring Chart’s process technology and LNG MCHE.
(208)    First, as explained in Sections 6.2.4.1.4 and 6.2.4.1.5, customers and competitors
         alike agreed these strategies are likely.

         foreclosure strategy, and the Parties can offer different commercial conditions on
         the projects on which they bid, such that a foreclosure strategy may focus on
         specific market segments where the strategy would be deemed the most profitable.
        This ability to discriminate reinforces the likelihood of incentives, given that even
            if such foreclosure would turn out not to be profitable on the market as a whole,
             it may well be profitable on certain market segments.
(210)   Third, the merged entity is unlikely to suffer many losses, due to its dominance in
     LNG compressor trains. The merged entity’s market shares in the target markets
         (heat exchangers and process technology) are also comparatively lower, allowing

         effective competition: through non-coordinated effects and through coordinated

         supplies or markets is hampered or eliminated as a result of the merger. (234)

       by restricting their access to an important input (input foreclosure), and (ii) where
         the merger is likely to foreclose upstream rivals by restricting their access to a

7.3.1.   Description of the Final Commitments
(326)  To address the shortcomings of the First Commitments, the Parties submitted an
       amended set of commitments on 6 July 2026 (the “Final Commitments”). In
          particular, the Parties amended the scope of and supporting provisions relating to
         the Divestment Business and the provisions of the Interoperability Obligations, as
         follows. (293)
(327)   The Final Commitments expand the scope of the Divestment Business to include
        Chart’s small-scale LNG process technology. Notably, this includes Chart’s four
        Chart process engineers with experience in small-scale process technology (294)
       and the know how related to small-scale process technology. (295) For IPSMR, the
        scope of patents is expanded to include all patents ‘primarily or exclusively’
         related  to IPSMR.  In  addition,  the  Final Commitments provide  that  the
        Divestment Business shall include all intellectual property (including patents,
         patent applications and knowhow), tangible assets, licences (including software
         licences), contracts, customer records, and copies of technical and commercial
        documentation relating to IPSMR and small-scale process technology (or the
         benefit of these assets, as appropriate depending on whether or not the assets are
         exclusively or primarily used for IPSMR or small-scale process technology). The
         Final Commitments also clarify that not only the net economic benefit of IPSMR
       and small-scale process technology will transfer to the Purchaser, but also that the
        Purchaser will benefit from adequate contractual arrangements to allow  it to
         interact directly with customers on existing LNG projects in providing the IPSMR
       and small-scale process technology services for those projects. Moreover, the
        scope of personnel included in the Divestment Business is expanded to include
       up to two Chart employees with expertise supporting IPSMR related functions,
            i.e. commercialisation and commissioning/start-up.
(328)   In the Final Commitments, the supporting provisions relating to the Divestment
        Business are amended to include a non-compete provision for three years after
         closing of the divestment, which prevents the merged entity from offering any
        process technology that would compete with IPSMR or small-scale process
        technology. Additionally, the Purchaser has the option to extend duration of the
         Transitional Support by 6 months. The Cold Box Supply Obligation is extended
         in duration to last up to 10 years after closing of the divestment.

7.3.2.   The Parties’ views
(331)   The Parties submit that the Final Commitments result in a Divestment Business
       and Interoperability Obligations that are effective and resolve the Commission’s
        concerns. (296) The Parties also submit that a number of potential purchasers have
        expressed interest and have already signed or are negotiating non-disclosure

7.3.3.   Assessment and conclusion on the Final Commitments
(332)  As explained in Section 7.2.3 above, the Market Test made clear that the First
       Commitments had certain key shortcomings with respect to the Divestment
        Business that undermined the effectiveness of the First Commitments. However,
             it is also apparent from the market test that if these issues would be addressed, the
        Divestment Business would result in a viable and attractive business, and the
       commitments could address the serious doubts that the Transaction would give
          rise to. The amendments introduced by the Parties into the Final Commitments
         resolve the concerns identified in the Market Test.
(333)   The scope of the Divestment Business has been significantly expanded to ensure
         that  it contains  all assets necessary for  its viability and competitiveness.  It
        includes the necessary tangible and intangible assets, staff, records and ongoing
         projects as well as Chart’s small-scale process technology capabilities for a
        Purchaser to compete effectively for the supply of LNG process technology in a
        timely manner. Moreover, the non-compete obligation resolves the concern that
         the merged entity could undermine the Divestment Business through re-entry in
     LNG process technology, by enabling it a sufficient period to establish its own
        presence in the market and gain customer trust. This objective is also supported
       by the extension of the maximum duration of the Transitional Support and Cold
      Box Supply Agreement. Requiring the Purchaser to be active in the LNG sector
        ensures they will have the necessary expertise and track record to successfully
         integrate and operate the Divestment Business. In addition, the adjustments to the
         Interoperability Obligations strengthen these Obligations and the protections for
         third  parties.  Accordingly, based on  the  information  available  to  it,  the
       Commission is satisfied that the Divestment Business is viable, competitive and
        marketable and the Interoperability Obligations are implementable and effective.

         the EEA Agreement.

        market is a condition, whereas the implementing steps which are necessary to
        achieve this result are generally obligations on the Parties. Where a condition is
        not fulfilled, the Commission’s decision declaring the concentration compatible
        with the internal market and the functioning of the EEA Agreement no longer
         stands. Where the undertakings concerned commit a breach of an obligation, the
       Commission may revoke the clearance decision in accordance with Article 6(3)(b)
        of the Merger Regulation. The undertakings concerned may also be subject to
         fines and periodic penalty payments under Articles 14(2) and 15(1) of the Merger
        Regulation.

         steps  that are necessary to achieve the modifications sought in a manner

SECTION G. DISPUTE RESOLUTION
57. The following dispute resolution procedure applies in case of conflict between the
   Committing Parties and the Purchaser in relation to the Commitments. The Committing
    Parties and the Purchaser shall appoint a panel of experts (the ‘Experts’). This panel shall
   comprise:

       (a) one expert appointed jointly by the Committing Parties;

       (b) one expert appointed by the Purchaser; and

       (c) one expert appointed by the two experts appointed under (a) and (b) provided that
             if they  fail to appoint the third expert within 15 working days from their
         appointment, either the Committing Parties or the Purchaser may request the
         Monitoring Trustee to appoint the third expert, provided that each person so
         appointed shall be independent of the Committing Parties and the Purchaser, and
         be a suitably qualified and experienced expert.

58. The process shall be conducted in private and shall be confidential but under supervision
    of the Monitoring Trustee. The language of the process shall be English.

59. The Experts shall act on the following basis:

       (a) the Experts shall act fairly and impartially;

       (b) each party shall submit to the Experts its brief and its submission in relation to the
         matter in dispute within five (5) working days of the Experts’ appointment;

       (c) the Experts shall decide the procedure to be followed within five (5) working days
          of their appointment, which may be the rules of arbitration of the London Court of
          International Arbitration;

       (d) the Committing Parties and the Purchaser shall assist and provide documentation
          as the Experts reasonably requires to consider the matters referred to them;

       (e) decisions of the Experts shall be based on majority votes of the panel;

        (f) the Experts’ determination in relation to any matter referred to them shall be given
         within a maximum period of one (1) month of the Experts’ appointment;

       (g) the Experts’ determination in relation to any matter referred to them shall (save
          for manifest error or fraud) be final and binding on the Committing Parties and the
          Purchaser;

       (h) any challenge to the Experts’ determination shall be made in the courts of Milan,
           Italy;

        (i) each party shall carry out the actions required to comply with the obligations set
         out in the Experts’ determination in relation to any matter pursuant referred to
        them within any time-limits specified by the Experts; and

           relation to any matter referred to it, including the fees and expenses of the Experts,

       (a) receiving all written submissions (including documents and reports, etc.) made by
